# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up answers the main open questions from the earlier documents well:
- It adds a second hours measure (system logs) to address unclaimed work.
- It registers the mediation test before the outcome data exist.
- It runs long enough to observe decay.
- It reports waiting times against control.
- It shows the four long-run studies in the meta-analysis were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.

The issues below are about consistency of measures, a contamination problem the authors don't connect to their own decay estimate, and some framing.

## 1. Arithmetic

**Checks out:**

| Figure | Check |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% |
| Per-hour gain, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% |
| Halden continuing organisations | 96.8 / (34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866) = +11.8% |
| Meeting-time DiD | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) = −3.3 h, same as at month 6 |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 |
| Counter staffing | Capacity ≈ 0.83 × 1.067 ≈ 0.886, so restoring it needs ~13% more staff, close to the county's 12% |

**Needs correcting:**
- **The Summary mixes measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months," but 12.5% is timesheet-based and 8.5% is log-based. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8% (timesheets), a fall of about 22%. Mixing the measures makes it look like 32%.
- **"Declined by about a quarter" (§5)** fits neither measure. It is about a fifth on timesheets and about a third if you mix in the log figure. Choose one measure and state it.

## 2. What do the log hours measure?

The paper describes log hours as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases." Taken literally, that means case work only, and meetings are not part of it. The figures then don't reconcile:

| | Treated |
|---|---|
| Total hours fall (timesheets, −12% of ~37.9) | ≈ 4.5 h |
| Recurring meetings fall (7.4 → 3.9) | 3.5 h |
| Implied fall in non-meeting time | ≈ 1.0 h |

If the logs record case work only, log hours should have fallen by only a few percent, not 11%.

There are two possibilities, and the authors need to say which applies:
- **Logs measure total working time** in some way, including meetings. Then the description needs correcting.
- **Logs measure case-work time only.** Then the −11% conflicts with the meeting data, and the mediation result means something different. Cutting meetings would not reduce case time, so the meetings pathway would have to work through less fragmentation rather than through time reallocation.

This also affects how the mediation result should be read. If the denominator includes meeting time, part of the "meetings pathway" is mechanical: time moves from meetings into case work, and output per total hour rises even if work per case-hour is unchanged. That is still a real gain in output per hour paid, and worth having. It is a different claim, though, from "meetings make people less productive."

Two smaller points on the logs:
- **Pre-period logs.** A difference-in-differences on log hours needs log data from before the trial. Say whether historical logs were available.
- **Level gap.** "Log data show slightly more work than timesheets" should be shown in hours per week, not only as a comparison of percentage falls.

## 3. Control-office contamination may explain part of the decay

The month-15 meeting audit in two control offices is reported only as a hint that reorganisation could deliver gains without cutting hours. It also bears directly on the decay estimate:
- If two of seven control offices improved output per hour by about 4% from month 15, the control-group average rises by about 1.2%. The treatment–control gap narrows by roughly that much **even if treated offices didn't fade at all**.
- Part of the 12.5% → 9.8% decline may therefore be control offices improving, not treated offices fading.
- Needed:
  - treated and control trajectories reported separately;
  - a sensitivity analysis that excludes the two auditing offices, or censors them at month 15.
- The audit was probably prompted by the trial itself, since control staff knew what treated offices were doing. That is a spillover, and it belongs in the Limitations.
- The "+4.1% against their own previous six months" is a before–after comparison. The other five control offices give you a comparison group for the same period, so a difference-in-differences is possible and should replace the before–after figure.

## 4. Mediation: "confirms" is too strong

- **Mediation is observational even within an RCT.** Randomisation assigned hours, not meeting cuts. Offices whose managers cut more meetings may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The Limitations say this, but the Summary's "confirms" doesn't. "Is consistent with" or "supports" would be accurate.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not office-months.** The phrase "a larger sample of office-months" suggests more independent information than exists. A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. Confirm that the CIs account for clustering, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
- **Registration timing.** The protocol was filed at month 11, after the exploratory meeting result and with 11 months of data already seen. That is still a fair confirmatory test of the 24-month data, but say it plainly.
- **The authors are testing their own hypothesis.** That is fine with registration, but independent replication matters more than usual here.

## 5. Gaps still left from the nine-month report

- **Backlogs.** The nine-month report said follow-up would show "whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines." This report doesn't address it. Include backlog size, time to decision and deadline breaches.
- **Primary outcome.** The registered primary outcome is output per FTE: −2.1% → −3.4%. It is drifting downward and not significant, and it should come first, ahead of the per-hour gains.
- **Cost in case-processing.** Cost is estimated for the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not for case-processing, where unchanged pay plus overtime must have raised cost per case.
- **Uncertainty.** There are still no CIs for appeal overturns, sick days or resignations. Appeal outcomes at 24 months are now meaningful, so test them.
- **Counter arm.** Report the full 12-month difference-in-differences for the counter offices: output per FTE, abandoned calls and repeat contacts. Ending the arm early because of service harm is a result in itself.

## 6. Halden subset

- **A third layer of selection.** These are organisations that submitted records, then agreed to the follow-up (14 of 23). The authors' caveat is good, but "upper bound" is stronger than the data allow. Unlogged work on the day off, which Varga–Holm noted, could still push the figure up. "Likely biased upward" is safer.
- **The work-type split isn't clean.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" includes a marketing agency that cited client deadlines. That is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Grouping it with coverage-bound settings stretches the category to fit the result. It is more honest to say one discretionary organisation also reverted, and why.
- **Time-tracking coverage.** Do all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking? Only 17 of the original 23 had both records and logs.
- **Conflict of interest.** R. Okafor, an author of the original pilot, is a co-author on the follow-up of those organisations. That should be declared, as should the Varden authors' role in proposing the meetings hypothesis now being tested.

## 7. §5 assessments of earlier claims

- **On Varga–Holm.** Fair. The 24-month estimate meets most of the standards they recommended, and a gain remains. Some fading is also visible, so their novelty concern was partly right, and §5 could say so as clearly as §3 does.
- **On the meta-analysis.** Correct, and decisive: four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies can't show whether effects decay. One qualification: if contamination accounts for part of the drop (§3 above), Varden's own decline is an upper estimate of how much the gain fades.

## Where the evidence now stands

> In randomised case-processing offices, output per log-measured hour remains about 8–10% higher than control at two years, down from 12.5% at nine months. Some of that decline may reflect control offices reorganising. Output per employee is about 3% lower, not statistically significant. Reduced meeting time is the largest measured correlate of the gain, and fatigue a smaller one. In coverage-bound work the scheme was abandoned because restoring service would have cost about 9% more per contact.

I can draft a consolidated synthesis across all five documents or a referee report on this one if useful.
